title: The round city
hookLine: the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad as a round city on the Tigris

lines: LINES OF ASH ON THE GROUND.
cards: Night, on the bank of the Tigris. Workers have marked out the plan of a city on the bare ground with lines of ash.
Now, al-Tabari reports, the caliph orders the lines laid over with cotton seeds soaked in naphtha, and set alight.
The whole plan of the city flares up in fire on the dark earth, so the caliph can walk it and see it whole before a single brick is laid. And the shape burning in the dark is a circle.
The caliph is al-Mansur, of the new Abbasid house, and the city is Baghdad. Today: the round city.

teach.b: Why a new city? The Abbasids had overthrown a dynasty based in Damascus, and their strength lay east, in Iraq and Khurasan. Al-Mansur wanted a capital of his own.
He chose a spot on the Tigris, where boats and roads could bring the trade of many lands, and gave it an official name: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace.
Some readers hear in it an echo of the Qur'an, where God is said to call people to the abode of peace. Then the shape.
The old descriptions tell of a city ringed by walls, with gates opening onto the great roads, each named for where its road led: the Kufa gate, the Basra gate, the Khurasan gate, the Syria gate.

At the very center stood the caliph's palace, crowned by a green dome, with the great mosque beside it. The ruler sits at the center, and the great roads of the empire run to his door: a city drawn as a picture of power.
Yet the circle didn't hold. Markets and neighborhoods spilled out past the walls almost from the start, and Baghdad grew in every direction, across the river and beyond.
The round city itself is long gone, known now only from the descriptions of writers who saw it or heard about it. A perfect circle, drawn in fire, and then the life of a real city overflowing it.

how: Historians reconstruct the round city of Baghdad from written descriptions by al-Tabari, al-Ya'qubi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, since little or nothing of it can be seen today.

practice: If you have paper and a pen, draw a circle as round as you can, knowing it won't be perfect, and put a dot at the center.

Ask what sits at the center of your days right now, work, worry, a person, a phone, and what you'd want there instead. If you pray, bring to mind the name the city was given, the City of Peace, and ask for peace in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mansur, the Abbasid caliph who had Baghdad's plan burned into the dark earth in lines of fire, and raised his round city on the Tigris around it. Today's word.
